_note: Baking: bread from flour and water in a masonry oven fired by process heat (Complaints/614). Cooks, tavern keepers and prepared-food service wait on the owner decision recorded in Complaints/530.

bread_kg.yield_basis: DOUGH AND BAKE. Flour takes up about two thirds of its weight in water to make bread dough (a hydration of about 65 percent: Wikipedia, Baker percentage, opened: 'medium hydration levels (58-65%) are typical for breads and rolls', so 65 is the top of the range; the baking loss, oven efficiency and labour were unsourced until Pass 11, see below): 690 kg of flour with 450 kg of water is about 1140 kg of dough, and the bake drives off about an eighth of that as steam, leaving about 1000 kg of loaves (Pass 11: forum bakers on The Fresh Loaf, https://www.thefreshloaf.com/node/23963, opened, report 8 to 10 percent total bake loss on loaves of 58 to 68 percent hydration, and William Rubel, https://williamrubel.com/all-about-wood-fired-bread-ovens/, opened, says a 68 kg batch of bread loses about 10 kg to evaporation, near 13 percent; an eighth is inside that range). Mass balance: 690 + 450 = 1140, less 140 evaporated. HEAT: the useful heat is warming the dough to boiling and evaporating the lost water, about 0.43 MJ plus 0.32 MJ a kilogram, near 0.8 MJ a kilogram of loaf; a wood-fired masonry oven delivers about an eighth of the fuel's heat to the dough (the rest heats the oven and flue; Pass 11: a measured wood-fired pizza oven had a thermal efficiency of 13 +- 4 percent, 'approximately 13%', Performance characterization of a traditional wood-fired pizza oven, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9804529/, opened, a modern analogue that the authors say is likely an overestimate; and wood-fired bakeries in Mozambique used 0.55 and 0.90 kg of wood per kg of wheat flour baked, Chalmers research page https://research.chalmers.se/en/publication/163260, opened: 6 MJ per kg of bread is 8.7 MJ per kg of flour, which is 0.55 kg of wood at an assumed 16 MJ per kg of dry wood, so the heat figure is in line), so about 6 MJ of thermal heat a kilogram, priced through the thermal_mj market at the oven's working temperature. LABOUR: kneading, shaping, loading and drawing the loaves, and tending the fire, about 60 baker-hours to a tonne of bread (a baker drawing two batches of about seventy kilograms a day; the batch size is supported by Rubel's 'one-hundred-fifty pounds of bread (68 kg) in a single batch' for a large wood oven, but the 60 baker-hours a tonne has no source found, so conf stays D). Round 3, archive.org text of a 1890s trade textbook, A text-book of the science and art of bread-making (https://archive.org/download/b29315104/b29315104_djvu.txt, opened): '4 lbs. 6 oz. of dough being taken for the 4 lb. loaf', a bake loss of 8.6 percent (inside the 8 to 10 percent above), 'about sixteen gallons' of water to a sack of flour and 'about ninety-one 4 lb. loaves to the sack of flour' (a sack is 280 lb in British trade, ASSUMED, not stated there), which is 91 x 4 / 280 = 1.3 kg of bread a kilogram of flour against 1000/690 = 1.45 here (within 12 percent); and of a small bakehouse with one peel oven the book says a trade of 'twenty-five sacks per week' is 'as much as is usually convenient to do in a one-oven bakehouse' (the text is a poor scan: 'tw eiity-five' sacks), which is 25 x 91 x 1.81 = 4100 kg of bread a week. Hours: the book gives no crew, so at an ASSUMED 60-hour week per hand, one hand over 4.1 tonnes is 60 / 4.1 = 14.6 hours a tonne, so the 60 hours a tonne here is about 4 hands, against the 2 or 3 a one-oven bakehouse would plausibly keep (assumption), within 2x; the crew is not sourced, so the hours stay D. OVEN: a domed brick oven is capital (below), not consumed. Calories are those of the flour: the satisfaction factor in data/world/needs.json is the flour's factor times the flour in a kilogram of bread, so baking adds no food energy.

capital.good: domed bread oven: brick vault, clay hearth, flue and door
capital.capital_basis: A bakery oven about two metres across is a vault of about a thousand bricks over a clay-and-brick hearth. Round 2 arithmetic: Forno Bravo forum poll, https://community.fornobravo.com/forum/pizza-oven-design-and-installation/pompeii-oven-construction/10272-poll-how-many-fire-bricks-did-you-use-for-your-oven, opened: builders of 42 inch (1.07 m) ovens report 260, 275 and about 280 firebricks for floor, dome and enclosure, and a 60 inch oven over 1,000 bricks of a smaller size. A dome's brick count goes with its area, so with the diameter squared: 270 x (2.0 / 1.07)^2 = about 940 bricks, which agrees with 1000 (assumption: a bakery oven built to the same one-brick-thick shape). Build hours (80 mason, 60 labourer) are still the author's estimate, no source found, conf D. Its vault is rebuilt after a decade or two of firing and cooling. A baker drawing two batches of about seventy kilograms on a working day for some three hundred days turns out about forty tonnes of loaves a year.
